These and other things I read in very many authors about magic and boys; but I am of doubtful judgment whether to say it can be so or to deny it — although I believe Plato when he holds that, between gods and men, certain powers of the divine, intermediate by nature and place, are set, and that these govern all divinations and the marvels of magicians; nay, I even reflect with myself that the human soul, and especially that of a boy, being simple, can, whether by the diversion of incantations or by the soothing of perfumes, be lulled to sleep, and estranged into a forgetfulness of present things, and, for a little while, the memory of the body being removed, be brought back and return to its own nature, which is, of course, immortal and divine, and so, as if in some slumber, foretell things to come. But in truth, however these matters stand, if any credit is to be given to such things, that prophetic boy — whoever he may be — ought, so far as I hear, to be chosen as both comely and unblemished in body and shrewd in mind and eloquent of speech, so that in him either the divine power may worthily lodge, as in a good house (if indeed it is enclosed in the boy's body), or his own soul, being roused, may be quickly brought back to its own power of divination, which, being readily implanted in it and wounded by no forgetfulness and dulled, may be easily resumed. For not from every wood, as Pythagoras used to say, ought a Mercury to be carved. If this is so, name the boy who was sound, unmaimed, gifted, comely, whom I thought worthy to initiate with a charm. But Thallus, whom you named, needs a physician rather than a magician; for the poor wretch is so wasted by the falling-sickness that, often three or four times a day, frequently without any incantations, he collapses, and racks all his limbs with convulsions, ulcerous of face, bruised on forehead and back of the head, dull of eye, gaping of nostril, faltering of foot. The greatest magician of all is he in whose presence Thallus has stood for any length of time: so generally, sinking with his malady as with sleep, does he topple over.

And yet you said that he was overthrown by my charms, because he happened once to fall down in my presence. Most of his fellow-slaves are present, whom you demanded to be produced. They can all tell you why they spit at the sight of Thallus, why no one dares to dine with him from the same dish or drink from the same cup. And why do I speak of slaves? You see them yourselves; deny that Thallus, long before I came to Oea, was wont to fall down with that malady, and was frequently shown to physicians; let his fellow-slaves, who are in your service, deny it: I will confess myself convicted of everything, unless... [the text is corrupt here] he was long ago banished to distant fields, that he might not contaminate the household: which that it was so done cannot even be denied by them. For this reason he could not be produced by us today. For as all this accusation was rash and sudden, two days ago Aemilianus served notice on us that we should produce fifteen slaves before you. Fourteen are present, who were in the town. Thallus alone, as I said, because he is far away in exile, about a hundred miles off — Thallus alone is absent, but we have sent someone to fetch him at full speed. Ask, Maximus, the fourteen slaves whom we produce, where the boy Thallus is and how well he is doing; ask the slaves of my accusers. They will not deny that he is a most loathsome boy, of rotten and diseased body, epileptic, barbarous, rustic. A fine boy you have chosen indeed, whom one might bring to a sacrifice, whose head one might touch, whom one might clothe in a pure cloak, from whom one might look for an oracle! By Hercules, I wish he were here: I would have handed him over to you, Aemilianus, and would have held him while you questioned him; already, in the middle of the inquiry, here, before the very tribunal, he would have turned his savage eyes upon you, foaming would have spat in your face, would have clenched his hands, shaken his head, and at last collapsed into your bosom.

The fourteen slaves you demanded I produce. Why do you not use them for any inquiry? You ask for one boy, and that an epileptic, whom you know to have long been absent, just as I do. What other slander is more evident? Fourteen slaves are present at your request, and you pretend not to see them; one little boy is absent, and him you arraign. Finally, what do you want? Suppose Thallus were present: do you want to prove that he fell down in my presence? I confess it of my own accord. Do you say it was done by a charm? Of this the boy knows nothing, and I refute that it was done; for that the boy is epileptic not even you will dare to deny. Why then should his falling be attributed to a charm rather than to his disease? Or could it not have happened that, by chance, in my presence, he suffered the same thing which he often suffered at other times in the presence of many? But if I thought it a great matter to throw down an epileptic, what need was there of a charm, when burnt jet-stone, as I read in the natural philosophers, beautifully and easily tests this disease — by whose smell men commonly try, even in slave-markets, the health or sickness of those for sale? Even a potter's wheel, whirled round, not without difficulty seizes a man of the same malady with its giddiness, so that the spectacle of its spinning weakens an already wounded mind; and a potter is far more potent to throw down epileptics than a magician. You demanded in vain that I produce slaves: I, not without cause, demand that you name what witnesses were present at this expiatory rite, when I, as you say, pushed the falling Thallus. You name one only, that little boy Sicinius Pudens, in whose name you accuse me; for he says that he was present. Even if his boyhood were no objection to the testimony's reliability, yet his being an accuser would rob it of credit. It would have been easier, Aemilianus, and far more telling, for you to say that you yourself were present and that from that rite you began to lose your wits, rather than to make over the whole business, as a child's plaything, to boys. A boy fell, a boy saw: did some boy, too, do the enchanting?

Here Tannonius Pudens, cunningly enough, when he saw that this lie too was growing cold and was now all but hissed off the stage by the looks and murmurs of all, in order to detain at least the suspicions of certain people by hope, said that he would produce other boys who had likewise been enchanted by me, and so passed over to another sort of argument. Which, although I might pretend not to notice, yet, as I do with everything, this too I challenge of my own accord. For I am eager that those boys be produced, whom, I hear, have been encouraged to lie by the hope of freedom. But I say no more: let them produce them. I demand, then, and insist, Tannonius Pudens, that you fulfil your promise. Bring forth those boys in whom you trust: produce them, name who they are. You may use my water-time for this. Speak, I say, Tannonius. Why are you silent, why do you delay, why do you look about you? But if this man does not know what he learned, or has forgotten the names, then you, Aemilianus, come forward, say what you charged your advocate to do, produce the boys. Why have you turned pale? Why are you silent? Is this to accuse, is this to lay so great a charge — or is it to make a mockery of Claudius Maximus, so great a man, and to harass me with slander? But if perchance your advocate has slipped in a word and you have no boys to produce, at least make some use of the fourteen slaves whom I produced.

Or why did you demand that so large a household be brought forward? Accusing me of magic, you served notice for fifteen slaves: why, if you were accusing me of violence, how many slaves, after all, would you demand? So then, fifteen slaves know something, and it is hidden. Or is it not hidden, and is it magic? You must necessarily confess one of these two things: either that the thing was not unlawful, in which I did not fear so many witnesses; or, if it was unlawful, that so many witnesses ought not to have known of it. This magic, as far as I hear, is a thing put under the ban of the laws, forbidden from of old by the Twelve Tables on account of incredible blightings of crops, and is therefore hidden no less than foul and horrible, generally kept watch through the nights and buried in darkness, solitary as to witnesses and muttered in incantations — to which not only few of slaves, but even few of free men, are admitted: and do you wish fifteen slaves to have been present? Was it a wedding, or some other crowded ceremony, or a seasonable banquet? Do fifteen slaves share in a magic rite, like the fifteen men appointed to perform the sacred rites? But for what purpose should I have admitted so many in number, if even a few are too many for a secret? Fifteen free men are a populace, as many slaves a household, as many fettered men a chain-gang. Or was their multitude necessary as a help, to hold the expiatory victims for a long time? But you named no victims except hens. Or was it to count the grains of incense, or to throw down Thallus?

You said, too, that a free woman, suffering from the same malady as Thallus, was brought to me at my house, whom I promised to cure, and that she too, enchanted by me, fell down. As I see, you have come to accuse a wrestling-master, not a magician: thus you say that all who came near me fell. Yet Themison the physician, by whom the woman was brought to me for inspection, denied — when you asked him, Maximus — that she suffered anything further than that I asked her whether her ears rang, and which of them more; and when she answered that her right ear was too much disturbed, I at once dismissed her. Here I, Maximus, although for the present I diligently refrain from your praises, lest anywhere, for the sake of this case, I should seem to flatter you, yet cannot but praise your shrewdness in questioning. For a while ago, when these things were being discussed, and they said the woman was enchanted, and the physician who had been present denied it, you asked, very prudently indeed, what profit there had been to me in enchanting her. They answered: "That the woman might fall." "What then? Did she die?" you say. They denied it. "What, then, do you say? What good did it do Apuleius, if she fell?" For so beautifully and persistently did you ask a third time, as one who knew that the reasons for all deeds must be more diligently examined, and that the causes are more often inquired into, while the deeds are granted; and that for this very reason the advocates of litigants are called pleaders of causes, because they set forth why each thing was done. But to deny a deed is an easy matter, and needs no advocate: to show that a deed was rightly or wrongly done — that, indeed, is far more arduous and difficult. In vain, then, is it inquired whether a thing was done, which had no bad cause for being done. So the man charged with a deed is freed, before a good judge, from the scruple of the inquiry, if he had no motive for sinning. Now, since they have proved the woman neither enchanted nor thrown down, and I do not deny that she was inspected by me at the physician's request, I will tell you, Maximus, why I asked that about the ringing of the ears — not so much to clear myself in that matter, which you have already prejudged to border on neither fault nor crime, as that I might not pass over in silence anything worthy of your ears and consonant with your learning. I will tell it, then, as briefly as I can; for you are to be reminded by me, not instructed.

Plato the philosopher, in that most illustrious "Timaeus," having framed the whole world with a certain heavenly eloquence — he, then, after he had most skilfully discoursed about the three powers of our soul too, and had most aptly taught why each of our members was fashioned for us by divine providence, reckons up the cause of all diseases under three heads. The first cause he assigns to the first elements of the body, if the very qualities of the elements — the moist and the cold, and the two opposite to these — do not agree; and this comes about when any one of them has either exceeded its measure or removed from its place. The next cause of diseases lies in the fault of those things which, already compounded from the simple elements, have nonetheless coalesced into one kind — such as the kind of blood, and of flesh, and of bone, and of marrow, and further, those things which are mixed from these single substances. Thirdly, in the body, the concretions of various bile and turbid breath and thick humour are the latest provokers of sicknesses.

Of which number the chief is the matter of the falling-sickness, of which I have begun to speak, when the flesh dissolves, by a hostile fire, into a thick and foaming humour, and, breath being generated from the same source, from the whiteness of the compressed air there flows a whitish and swollen corruption. For if that corruption breathes out to the exterior of the body, it spreads with more disgrace than harm; for it marks the outer skin of the breast with white blotches and varies it with every kind of stain. But whoever this has befallen is never afterward attacked by the falling-sickness; thus he balances a most grievous sickness of the mind by a slight disfigurement of the body. But if that pernicious sweetness, held within and joined with black bile, has raged and spread through all the veins, and then, having forced a way to the topmost head, has mingled its dread flux with the brain, it forthwith weakens the royal part of the soul, which, strong in reason, has taken its seat in the crown of a man's head as in a citadel and palace. For it overwhelms and disturbs its divine ways and wise passages; which it does with less harm during sleep, when it presses, with a moderate strangling that is the forerunner of the falling-sickness, those who are full of drink and food. But if it has so far increased that it is poured even over the head of the waking, then indeed, by a sudden clouding of the mind, they grow numb, and, the body dying, the soul failing, they fall. This our people have truly named not only the major sickness and the falling-sickness, but even the divine sickness — just as the Greeks call it the "sacred disease" — namely because it does violence to the rational part of the soul, which is by far the most holy.

You recognize, Maximus, Plato's reasoning, expounded as clearly as I could for the occasion; and I, trusting it, and judging the cause of the divine sickness to be when that plague has flowed back into the head, do not at all seem to have inquired about nothing when I asked whether that woman had a heavy head, a stiff neck, throbbing temples, ringing ears. But that she confessed the more frequent ringings in her right ear was a sign that the disease was driven deep within; for the right parts of the body are the stronger, and therefore leave the less hope of recovery when they too succumb to sickness. Aristotle indeed left it written in his "Problems" that, in whatever epileptics the disease begins from the right, theirs is the harder to cure. It would be tedious, if I wished to review Theophrastus' opinion too about the same disease; for he too has an excellent book on epileptics. To whom, nonetheless, in another book, which he wrote on grudging animals, he says that the cast skins of geckos are a remedy — which they cast off, like old age, after the manner of other serpents, at fixed seasons; but unless you snatch them away at once, whether by malignant foreknowledge or by natural appetite, they straightway turn and devour them. I have mentioned these things on this account, and have diligently named at once the discussions and the books of noble philosophers, and have wished to touch upon none of the physicians or the poets, that these men may cease to wonder if philosophers, by their own learning, know the causes of diseases and their remedies. Therefore, since a sick woman was brought to me to be inspected for the sake of treatment, and since it is agreed, both by the confession of the physician who brought her to me and by my own reasoning, that this was rightly done, either let them lay it down that to cure diseases belongs to a magician and a malefactor, or, if they dare not say this, let them confess that, in the case of the epileptic boy and woman, they have leveled empty and utterly tumbling slanders.

Nay rather, if you would have the truth, Aemilianus, you are the epileptic one, who have already fallen by so many slanders. For it is no graver to collapse in body than in heart, to topple over with the foot rather than with the mind, to be spat upon in the bedchamber than to be execrated in this most splendid assembly. But you, perhaps, think yourself sound, because you are not kept at home, but follow your madness wherever it has led you. And yet match, if you will, your own frenzy with the frenzy of Thallus: you will find no great difference, except that Thallus rages against himself, while you rage against others too. For the rest, Thallus rolls his eyes, you the truth; Thallus clenches his hands, you your advocates; Thallus is dashed against the pavements, you against the tribunals; finally, he does whatever he does in sickness, and sins unknowingly: but you, wretch, offend knowingly and wittingly, so great is the force of the disease that goads you on; you allege the false for the true, you make a crime of the undone as of the done, the man whom you clearly know to be innocent you nevertheless accuse as guilty.

There is more besides — a point I passed over. There are things you admit you do not know, and yet these same things you make a charge of, as if you knew them. For you say that I kept certain objects wrapped in a little linen cloth among the household gods of Pontianus. What those wrapped things were, and of what kind, you confess you do not know, nor is there anyone else who saw them; yet you maintain they were the instruments of magic. Let no one flatter you, Aemilianus: there is no cunning in this accusing of yours, nor even any impudence — lest you should think there is. What is it, then? It is the wretched frenzy of an embittered mind, and the pitiable madness of a raw and unripe old age. For in pretty nearly these words you addressed a judge so weighty and so clear-sighted: "Apuleius kept certain things wrapped in a bit of linen among the household gods of Pontianus. Since I do not know what these things were, on that very account I maintain that they were magical. Believe me, then, in what I say, because I say what I do not know." What splendid arguments, and how plainly they convict the accused! "It was so, since I do not know what it was." You alone, Aemilianus, have been found out to know even the things you do not know; so far above all men have you been carried in your folly — seeing that the most skilful and acute of the philosophers say that not even the things we see are to be trusted, while you make assertions even about the things you have neither ever beheld nor heard of. If Pontianus were alive and you were to question him as to what was in that wrapping, he would answer that he did not know. There stands the freedman who to this day holds the key of that place and stands on your side: he says that he never looked inside, although he himself opened it, being the keeper of the books that were stored there, almost daily, and shut it again; that he often went in with us, much oftener alone; that he saw the linen lying on the table without any seal, without any fastening. And why not? Magical articles were being hidden inside it: I kept it all the more carelessly for that, I exposed it carelessly to be freely searched and inspected at pleasure, even to be carried off, I entrusted it to another's keeping, I left it to another's discretion. What, then, do you wish to be believed at this present? That the thing which Pontianus did not know — Pontianus, who lived with me in an unbroken intimacy — is known to you, whom I never saw except before the tribunal? Or that what the freedman, constantly at hand and with every opportunity of inspecting it, did not see, you saw — you who never came near the place? Finally, grant that what you did not see was such as you say: yet, you fool, if today you had intercepted that little cloth, whatever you produced out of it, I should deny was magical.

I even allow you this: imagine whatever you like, invent it, devise something that could appear magical: yet even so I would contend with you about it. I should say either that it had been planted, or received as a remedy, or handed down in a religious rite, or enjoined in a dream; there are a thousand other grounds on which I could refute you truly, by common usage and the most familiar custom of religious observance. As it is, you demand that a thing which, even if it had been seized and held, would nevertheless do me no harm before a good judge, should condemn me on the strength of an empty suspicion, uncertain and unknown. Perhaps you will say again, as you are wont: "What, then, was that which you wrapped in linen and laid up, of all places, among the household gods?" Is that your way, Aemilianus? Do you accuse like this — questioning the defendant about everything, bringing forward nothing ascertained yourself? "Why do you look for fish? Why did you examine a sick woman? What did you keep in the cloth?" Did you come to accuse or to interrogate? If to accuse, then prove the things you say yourself; if to interrogate, do not pronounce beforehand what the thing was, since you are obliged to ask precisely because you do not know. But indeed, on these terms all men will be set up as defendants, if the man who has lodged an information against anyone is under no necessity of proving it, while he has every facility of questioning. For in this way, just as a charge of magic is fastened on someone, anything at all that a man may have done will be thrown in his teeth. "You set the mark of a vow on the thigof some statue: therefore you are a magician; or else, why did you mark it? You offered silent prayers to the gods in a temple: therefore you are a magician; or else, what did you pray for?" On the other hand: "You prayed for nothing in the temple: therefore you are a magician; or else, why did you not entreat the gods?" In like manner, if you have set down some offering, if you have sacrificed, if you have taken a sprig of vervain. The day would fail me, if I wished to follow out all the things for which a slanderer would in the same way demand a reason. Especially as everything whatsoever that is stored, that is sealed, that is shut away and kept in the house, will all, by the same argument, be called magical, or be dragged out of the storeroom into the forum and into court.

How great these matters are, and of what kind, Maximus, and how wide a field is opened to slander by this path of Aemilianus, and what sweats are brought upon the innocent by this one little cloth, I could indeed dispute at greater length; but I will do what I set out to do: I will confess even what is not necessary, and, when questioned by Aemilianus, I will answer. You ask, Aemilianus, what I kept in the cloth. Now, although I could altogether deny that any cloth of mine was placed in the library of Pontianus, and, even if I were to grant fully that there was one, could still say that nothing was wrapped in it — and if I were to say this, I could be refuted neither by any testimony nor by any argument, for there is no one who touched it, the one freedman, as you say, who saw it — yet, I say, for all I care, let it have been crammed full. Think of it so, if you will, as once the companions of Ulysses thought they had found a treasure, when they were pilfering a bag full of nothing but wind. Do you wish me to tell you what sort of things they were that I wrapped in the cloth and entrusted to the household gods of Pontianus? Your wish shall be granted. I have shared in very many sacred initiations in Greece. Certain tokens and memorials of these, given to me by the priests, I diligently preserve. I say nothing unusual, nothing unknown. Even the initiates of Father Liber alone, you who are present, know what you keep hidden at home and venerate in silence apart from all the uninitiated. But I, as I said, have learned manifold sacred rites, very many ceremonies, and various religious observances, out of zeal for truth and duty toward the gods. Nor do I compose this for the occasion; for it is now about three years since, in the first days after I had come to Oea, discoursing in public on the majesty of Aesculapius, I declared these same things openly and recounted how many rites I knew. That discourse is most widely current, is commonly read, passes through everyone's hands, commended to the devout people of Oea not so much by my eloquence as by the mention of Aesculapius. Let someone say, if anyone perhaps remembers, the opening of that passage. — Do you hear, Maximus, the many who prompt it? Why, look, the very book is offered me. I will order these very words to be read out, since you show

by your most kindly look that you do not find such a hearing burdensome. — Can it then seem strange to anyone who has any recollection of religion, that a man initiated into so many mysteries of the gods should keep at home certain holy tokens of the sacred rites, and should wrap them in a linen cloth, which is the purest of coverings for things divine? For wool, the sluggish body's excrement, stripped from the sheep, is from the very precepts of Orpheus and Pythagoras a profane garment; whereas the spotless crop of flax, sprung from the earth among the choicest of fruits, is used by the most holy priests of the Egyptians not only for clothing and covering, but for veiling sacred things as well. And I know that some men, and chief among them this Aemilianus, make a jest of mocking things divine. For, as I hear from some of the people of Oea who know him, he has to this day made supplication to no god, has frequented no temple; if he passes any shrine, he counts it a sin to lift his hand to his lips in reverence. Indeed, even to the gods of husbandry, who feed and clothe him, he gives no first-fruits of any crop or vine or flock; in his farm stands no chapel, no place or grove is consecrated. Why do I speak of grove and chapel? Those who have been there say they have not seen even one anointed stone or one garlanded bough within his borders. Two surnames, therefore, have been bestowed on him: Charon, as I said already, for the grimness of his face and his temper; but the other, which he hears with more pleasure, for his contempt of the gods — Mezentius. And so I readily understand that these enumerations of so many initiations seem to him mere trifles, and that perhaps, out of this defiance of the divine, he cannot bring himself to think true what I have said — that I keep, most reverently, the tokens and memorials of so many sacred rites. But I would not turn my hand for what Mezentius thinks of me; to the rest, however, I declare in the clearest voice: if anyone is present who shares in those same solemnities of mine, let him give the sign, and you may hear what things I keep. For I, in truth, shall never be driven by any peril to divulge to the profane what I have received under the seal of silence.

As I think, Maximus, I seem to have satisfied the mind of anyone, even the most hostile, and, as regards the cloth, to have wiped away every stain of the charge; and now, with good warrant of safety, I am ready to pass from the suspicions of Aemilianus to that testimony of Crassus which they read out after these matters as if it were the weightiest of all. You heard read from a written deposition the testimony of a certain glutton and desperate gormandizer, Junius Crassus, that I had repeatedly performed nocturnal rites in his house, together with my friend Appius Quintianus, who lodged there for hire. And this, Crassus says, although at that time he was actually at Alexandria, he yet learned from the smoke of the torch and the feathers of birds. To be sure, while he was making the round of the drinking-parties at Alexandria — for this Crassus is a man who not unwillingly creeps off by daylight into the cookshops — in that reek of the tavern he caught, like a fowler, the feathers wafted from his own household gods, and recognized the smoke of his own house, risen afar from his ancestral roof. If he saw it with his eyes, then he is more keen-sighted than the prayers and longings of Ulysses; for Ulysses, gazing for many years from the shore for the smoke rising from his own land, vainly strained to catch it; but Crassus, in the few months of his absence, saw that same smoke without any effort, sitting in a wine-shop. Or if, on the other hand, he perceived the reek of his own house with his nostrils, then again he surpasses dogs and vultures in keenness of scent; for to what dog, to what vulture of the Alexandrian sky, could anything smell all the way from the borders of Oea? This Crassus is indeed a consummate gormandizer, and not unskilled in every kind of smoke; but assuredly, given his zeal for drinking, by which alone he is reckoned, the breath of wine would reach him at Alexandria more easily than that of smoke.

He understood himself that this would seem incredible; for it is said that before the second hour of the day, still fasting and unfortified with wine, he sold that testimony. So he wrote that he had learned these things in this manner: that after he returned from Alexandria, he made straight for his house, from which Quintianus had already moved out; that there, in the vestibule, he came upon many birds' feathers, and besides that the walls disfigured with soot; that he asked the reason of his slave, whom he had left behind at Oea, and the slave informed him about the nocturnal rites of myself and Quintianus. But how cunningly contrived it is, and how plausibly invented, that I, if I had wished to do anything of the sort, would not rather have done it in my own house; that this Quintianus, who stands beside me — whom I name, for honour's and praise's sake, on account of the very close friendship I have with him, and on account of his outstanding learning and most perfect eloquence — that this Quintianus, then, if he had had any birds at dinner, or, as they say, had killed any for magic's sake, had no slave-boy to sweep up the feathers and throw them outside; and besides, that the force of the smoke was so great as to make the walls black, and that Quintianus endured this disfigurement in his bedchamber as long as he lived there. You say nothing, Aemilianus; it is not plausible — unless perhaps Crassus, on his return, did not make straight for his bedchamber, but, after his manner, went directly to the kitchen hearth. But from what did Crassus's slave conjecture that the walls had been smoked precisely at night? Was it from the colour of the smoke? No doubt night-smoke is blacker, and so differs from day-smoke. And why did so suspicious and so diligent a slave allow Quintianus to move out before he had restored the house to cleanliness? Why did those feathers, as if of lead, await the coming of Crassus so long? Let Crassus not lay the charge upon his slave: he himself rather invented all this about the soot and the feathers, since not even in giving testimony can he get any farther from the kitchen.

But why was the testimony read from a written deposition? Where in the world is Crassus himself? Has he gone back to Alexandria out of weariness of his house? Is he scrubbing his walls? Or, what is nearer the truth, is the gormandizer laid low by a debauch? For I myself yesterday, here at Sabrata, noticed him very conspicuously belching at you, Aemilianus, in the middle of the forum. Ask your nomenclators, Maximus — although he is better known to the tavern-keepers than to the nomenclators — yet, I say, inquire whether they have seen this Junius Crassus of Oea; they will not deny it. Let Aemilianus produce to us this most honourable youth, on whose testimony he relies. You see what time of day it is: I say that Crassus has long since been snoring drunk, or, after a second bath taken to enable him to attend the after-dinner carousal, is sweating out his wine-soaked perspiration in the baths. He speaks to you, Maximus, present though absent, through a written deposition — not but that he is so utterly lost to all shame that, even if he were under your eyes, he would lie without any blush; but perhaps he could not so much as restrain himself in his tippling to await this hour sober: or rather, Aemilianus did it of set purpose, that he might not station him under your so stern eyes, lest you should reject that brute, with his plucked jaws and foul aspect, on the very sight of his face, when you had observed the youth's head ravaged of beard and hair, his rheumy eyes, his swollen eyelids, his gaping mouth, his slobbering lips, his discordant voice, the trembling of his hands, his belching breath. His whole patrimony he licked away long ago, and nothing remains to him of his father's goods but one house, fit for retailing slander, which yet he never let out at a dearer rate than for this testimony; for that drunken lie he sold to this Aemilianus for three thousand sesterces, and there is no one at Oea who is ignorant of it.

We all knew of this before it was done, and I could have hindered it by a formal protest, had I not known that a lie so foolish would harm Aemilianus, who was buying it to no purpose, rather than me, who deservedly despised it. I wished both that Aemilianus should suffer the loss and that Crassus should be set up for prostitution by the disgrace of his testimony. For the rest, the affair was carried through, the day before yesterday, by no means in secret, in the house of one Rufinus — of whom I shall speak presently — Rufinus himself and Calpurnianus acting as go-betweens and intercessors. And Rufinus accomplished this all the more gladly because he was sure that Crassus would pass on no small part of his reward to his wife, whose adulteries he knowingly winks at. I saw that you too, Maximus, in your wisdom, suspecting their cabal and conspiracy against me the moment that deposition was brought forward, spurned the whole business with your countenance. In short, although they are endowed with an unusual audacity and a troublesome impudence, yet — seeing that the testimony of Crassus had, as they perceived, smelt of the lees — they themselves did not dare to read it through, nor to lean upon it for anything. But I have recalled these things, not because I feared, with you for judge above all, the scarecrows of feathers and the stain of soot, but that it might not go unpunished in Crassus that he sold gross smoke to Aemilianus, a country bumpkin.

One charge more was brought forward by them, when they were reading the letters of Pudentilla, concerning the fashioning of a certain little statue, which they say I had procured for magical sorceries, made of the choicest wood by a secret craft, and which, although it is in the shape of a skeleton, foul and horrible, I yet cultivate at great cost and call by the Greek name "king." Unless I am mistaken, I am following their footsteps in order, and, taking each point one by one, I am unweaving the whole web of slander. The fashioning of the statue, which you call secret, how can it have been secret, when you were so far from being ignorant of its maker that you summoned him to be present here? See, here is Cornelius Saturninus, the craftsman, a man both praised among his fellows for his art and approved for his character, who a little while ago, when you questioned him diligently, Maximus, recounted the whole course of the matter to you with the utmost good faith and truth: how I, when I had seen at his shop many geometrical figures of boxwood, finely and skilfully made, being attracted by his craftsmanship, asked him to work out for me certain mechanical contrivances, and at the same time to carve me some image, of whatever god he liked, to which I might make supplication after my custom, of whatever material, provided only it was of wood. So at first he tried boxwood. Meanwhile, while I was in the country, my stepson Sicinius Pontianus, who wished it done for me, obtained some little caskets of ebony from a most honourable lady, Capitolina, brought them to him, and urged him to make it rather of that rarer and more durable material; that gift would be especially welcome to me. He did accordingly, as far as the caskets sufficed. And so, fitted together piece by piece out of the little tablets to a certain thickness, a little Mercury could be wrought.

All this, as I say, you have heard. Moreover, the same things were said by the son of Capitolina, a most upright young man, who is present, when you questioned him: that Pontianus had asked for the caskets, that Pontianus had brought them to Saturninus the craftsman. Nor is even this denied — that Pontianus received the finished statue from Saturninus, and afterward gave it to me as a gift. All these things being proved openly and plainly, what at all remains in which any suspicion of magic can lurk? Nay, what is there at all that does not convict you of manifest falsehood? You said that the thing was secretly made which Pontianus, a most distinguished knight, saw to the making of; which Saturninus, a man of weight and well known among his fellows for his honesty, carved openly, sitting in his own shop; which a most accomplished matron helped with her gift; which both before and after the making was known to many, both of the slaves and of the friends who used to come to me. The wood, that I sought through the whole town — and indeed sought hard for it — you were not ashamed to make up, though you know I was away at that time, though it has been proved that I ordered it to be made of whatever material.

Your third falsehood was that there had been fashioned a lean, nay an utterly disembowelled, shape of a grim corpse, downright horrible and ghoulish. Now if you had ascertained so evident a sign of magic, why did you not formally call on me to produce it? Was it that you might be free to lie about a thing that was not there? Yet the means of that falsehood was taken from you by a certain happy chance of my habit. For I make it my custom, wherever I go, to carry the image of some god hidden among my books, and on feast-days to make supplication to it with incense and wine and sometimes a victim. So just now, when I heard a "skeleton" so impudently and so falsely talked of again and again, I bade someone go at a run and fetch from my lodging the little Mercury which this Saturninus fashioned for me at Oea. Hand it over, you — let them see it, hold it, examine it. There you have what that wretch called a skeleton. Do you hear the outcry of all who are present? Do you hear the condemnation of your falsehood? Are you not at last ashamed of so many slanders? Is this a skeleton, is this a ghoul, is this what you kept calling a demon? Is this image magical, or solemn and ordinary? Take it, I pray you, Maximus, and contemplate it: it is well that a consecrated thing should be handed to hands so pure and so pious as yours. See how comely its face is, and full of the bloom of the wrestling-school; how cheerful the god's countenance; how gracefully the down creeps over either cheek; how the curled hair appears on his head beneath the rim of his cap; how prettily the two little wings stand out above his temples; how festively the garment is gathered up about his shoulders. The man who dares to call this a skeleton assuredly either sees no images of the gods at all, or neglects them all; and the man, finally, who thinks this a ghoul is himself the ghoul-haunted one.

But to you, Aemilianus, in return for that falsehood, may that god who is the messenger between the powers above and below grant the ill-will of both sets of gods, and ever set before your eyes the shapes of the dead to meet you, whatever there is anywhere of shades, whatever of spectres, whatever of departed spirits, whatever of ghouls — all the apparitions of the night, all the terrors of the funeral pyre, all the frights of the tomb — from which, for all that, in age and in desert you are not far off. But we of the Platonic household know nothing but what is festive and joyful and solemn and lofty and heavenly. Indeed, in its zeal for the heights, that school has explored certain things even loftier than heaven itself, and has stood on the outermost back of the universe. Maximus knows that I speak the truth, who has read in the Phaedrus, diligently, of "the place beyond the heavens" and "the back of heaven." The same Maximus understands very well — to answer you about the name also — who that "king" is, named so not first by me but by Plato: "About the king of all things are all things, and for his sake are all things" — who that king is, the cause and reason and original source of all the nature of things, the supreme begetter of the soul, the everlasting preserver of living creatures, the unwearied maker of his own world, yet a maker without labour, a preserver without care, a begetter without propagation; comprehended by no place, no time, no change whatever, and therefore conceivable by few, expressible by none.

Look, I freely heighten the suspicion of magic: I do not answer you, Aemilianus, what "king" it is that I worship; nay, if the proconsul himself should ask me what my god is, I keep silence. Of the name I have for the present said enough. As for what remains, I myself am not unaware that some of the bystanders desire to hear why I chose to have my image made not of silver or gold, but of wood above all; and this, I think, they desire not so much to find fault as to learn, that they may be freed from this scruple too, when they see every suspicion of the charge abundantly confuted. Hear, then, you whose care it is to learn — but with your mind as upright and attentive as you can make it, as though you were about to hear the very words of Plato, now an old man, from the last book of the Laws: "A man of measure, in dedicating offerings to the gods, ought to give measured ones. The earth, then, and the hearth of every dwelling are sacred to all men, of all the gods; let no one, therefore, consecrate sacred things to the gods a second time" — this he forbids in order that no one may dare to set up shrines privately; for he holds it enough that the citizens have public temples for the immolation of victims — then he adds: "Gold and silver, in other cities, both in private hands and in temples, are a possession that breeds envy; ivory, from a body that has left its soul behind, is no gracious offering; iron and bronze are instruments of war; but of wood, let a man dedicate whatever he will, made of a single block, and of stone likewise." As the assent of all has declared, Maximus, and you who sit in council, I seem to have used Plato most fittingly, as the master of my life, so the patron of my cause, to whose laws you see me obedient.

Now it is time to turn beforehand to the letters of Pudentilla — or rather to fetch the whole order of the matter from a little higher up, so that it may lie open most plainly to all that I, who they keep saying invaded the house of Pudentilla out of greed for gain, ought, if I had thought of any gain at all, always to have fled from that house, since in other respects too the match was anything but prosperous — indeed, hostile to me, had not the woman herself balanced so many disadvantages by her virtues. For no other cause can be found, save empty envy, which has kindled against me both this trial and, before it, many perils of my life. For why should Aemilianus be moved, even if he had truly found me out to be a magician — a man who has been injured by no deed of mine, nor by so much as the slightest word of mine, that he should seem to be going to avenge himself deservedly? Nor again does he accuse me for glory's sake, as Marcus Antonius accused Gnaeus Carbo, Gaius Mucius accused Aulus Albucius, Publius Sulpicius accused Gnaeus Norbanus, Gaius Furius accused Manius Aquilius, Gaius Curio accused Quintus Metellus. For those most learned young men undertook this, the first exercise of their forensic labour, for praise's sake, that by some notable prosecution they might become known to their fellow-citizens. This custom, granted among the ancients to young beginners as a means of displaying the flower of their talent, has long since fallen into disuse. And even if it were now common, still it would have been far from this fellow; for neither would a parade of eloquence have suited an unlettered and ignorant man, nor a desire of glory a rustic and a barbarian, nor the undertaking of advocacies an old man at the grave's edge — unless, perhaps, Aemilianus, true to his severity, has set an example, and, out of hatred for the very crimes themselves, has taken up this accusation for the integrity of his morals. But this I could scarcely have believed of Aemilianus — not this African here, but that famous Africanus and Numantinus and Censorius besides: let me not believe of this stump of a man that he has in him not only hatred of misdeeds, but even the understanding of them.

What is it, then? It is clearer than anything to anyone that there is no other cause but envy which has spurred this man, and Herennius Rufinus, his instigator (of whom I shall speak presently), and the rest of my enemies, to weave together these slanders of magic. There are, then, five points which I must discuss. For, if I remember rightly, as regards Pudentilla they brought these charges: one point is that they said she had never wished to marry after her former husband, but was compelled by my incantations; the second is about her letter, which they take for a confession of magic; then, that she married at the sixtieth year of her age out of lust, and that the marriage-contract was sealed in a country house and not in town — these they brought up in the third and fourth place; the last, and likewise the most envy-laden, accusation was about the dowry. There they strove, with all their strength, to pour out all their venom; there above all they were tortured; and so they said that I extorted a great dowry, at the very beginning of our union, from a woman in love, with the witnesses removed, in a country house. All these things I shall show to be so false, so worthless, so empty, and shall refute them so easily and without any contention, that, so help me, I fear, Maximus, and you who sit in council, lest you should think the accuser was sent down and suborned by me, that, finding the occasion, I might openly extinguish the envy against me. Believe me — which the fact itself will make clear — I have to labour exceedingly hard, lest you should suppose that I cunningly devised so frivolous an accusation rather than that they foolishly undertook it.

Now, while I briefly follow out the order of the matter and bring it about that Aemilianus himself, when the matter is known, must needs confess that he was led into envy of me on false grounds and went far astray from the truth, I pray you, as you have done hitherto, or even more closely if you can, attend most diligently to the very source and foundation of this trial. Aemilia Pudentilla, who is now my wife, bore, by a certain Sicinius Amicus, to whom she had previously been married, two sons, Pontianus and Pudens; and these, left orphans in the power of their paternal grandfather — for Amicus had died while his father survived — she reared diligently, with memorable devotion, for about fourteen years, yet not gladly a widow so long in the very flower of her age. But the boys' grandfather strove to betroth her, against her will, to his other son, Sicinius Clarus, and on that account frightened off the other suitors; and besides he threatened that, if she married a stranger, he would leave her sons nothing of their father's goods by his will. When the wise and singularly devoted woman saw this condition obstinately laid down, lest she should in any way harm her sons on that score, she does indeed draw up a marriage-contract with the man she was bidden to marry, with Sicinius Clarus, but in very truth, by various delays, she eludes the marriage until the boys' grandfather yielded to fate, leaving her sons his heirs in such wise that Pontianus, who was the elder, should be guardian to his brother.

Freed from that scruple, when she was sought in marriage by men of the first rank, she resolved that she ought not to remain longer in widowhood; for, though she could endure the weariness of solitude, she could not bear the sickness of her body. A woman chastely modest, through so many years of widowhood without fault, without scandal, grown torpid through want of a husband and wounded by the long stagnation of her inward parts, with the inmost recesses of her womb corrupted, she was often, when pains arose, brought to the very brink of life. The physicians, together with the midwives, were agreed that the disease was caused by the lack of marriage, that the malady was growing worse day by day, that the sickness was deepening; while some bloom of her age remained, the disorder must be remedied by marriage. This counsel both others approved, and Aemilianus here above all — the very man who a little while ago, with most confident falsehood, asserted that Pudentilla had never thought of marriage before she was compelled by magical sorceries by me; that I alone had been found to violate, with charms and poisons, the as-it-were virginity of her widowhood. I have often heard it said, and not without reason, that a liar ought to have a good memory; but it did not come into your mind, Aemilianus, that, before I came to Oea, you yourself had even written letters urging her to marry, to her son Pontianus, who was then grown up and living at Rome. Produce the letter — or rather, give it to him himself: let him read it, let him convict himself by his own voice and his own words. Is this your letter? Why have you turned pale? For blush you certainly cannot. Is this your signature? — Read it, I pray you, more loudly, that all may understand how much his tongue is at variance with his hand, and how much less he is at odds with me than with himself.

Did you write these things, Aemilianus, which have been read? "That she wishes and ought to marry, I know; but whom she is to choose, I do not know." Quite right of you: you did not know; for Pudentilla, who knew well your hostile malignity, confessed to you only the fact itself, but nothing about the suitor. But you, while you thought she would still be married to your brother Clarus, led on by a false hope, were even an adviser to his son Pontianus too to give his consent. And so, if she had married Clarus, a country fellow and a decrepit old man, you would say she had married long ago of her own accord, without any magic; but since she chose a young man such as you describe, you say she did it under compulsion, and otherwise had always spurned marriage. You did not know, you scoundrel, that your letter on this subject was being kept; you did not know that you would be convicted by your own testimony. Yet that letter, the witness and informer of your purpose, Pudentilla — knowing you to be light and changeable, and no less lying and impudent — chose to keep rather than to send back. As for the matter itself, she herself wrote to her son Pontianus at Rome, and fully set forth the reasons of her resolve as well. She told him all about her health: that there was nothing besides, why she should hold out any longer; that she had sought her grandfather's inheritance by a long widowhood, with contempt of her own well-being, and had increased that same inheritance by the utmost industry; that now, by the will of the gods, he himself was of an age for a wife, and his brother for the manly toga; that they should at last allow her too to relieve her solitude and her sickness; for the rest, that they should fear nothing concerning her devotion and her final disposition: that, such as she had been to them as a widow, such would she be as a wife. I will order a copy of this letter, sent to her son, to be read out.

I think it can be plain enough to anyone from these things that Pudentilla was not driven from a stubborn widowhood by my incantations, but, having long since of her own accord been by no means averse from marriage, perhaps preferred me before the rest. And why this choice of so weighty a woman ought to be made a charge against me rather than an honour, I cannot discover; only I wonder that Aemilianus and Rufinus take so ill this judgment of the woman, when those very men who sought Pudentilla in marriage bear it with an even mind that I was preferred to them. And indeed, that she did this, she obeyed her son rather than her own heart. So it was done, nor will Aemilianus be able to deny it. For Pontianus, on receiving his mother's letter, flew at once from Rome, fearing lest, if she had got hold of some greedy husband, she might, as often happens, carry everything off into her husband's house. That anxiety gnawed his mind not a little: all the hopes of riches for him and his brother lay in their mother's resources. Their grandfather had left them a modest sum; their mother possessed four million sesterces, of which she owed a certain amount of money to her sons, received under no written deed, but, as was fair, on her mere good faith. This fear he muttered to himself; he did not dare to oppose her openly, lest he should seem to distrust her.

When matters stood thus, between the mother's wooing and the son's fear, by chance or by fate, I arrive, on my way to Alexandria. By Hercules, I would have said "would that it had never happened," did not regard for my wife forbid me. It was the winter of the year. I, worn out by the fatigue of the journey, take to my bed for a good many days at the house of those friends of mine, the Appii, whom I name out of honour and affection. Thither came Pontianus to me; for he had been brought into acquaintance with me not so very long before, many years ago, at Athens, through certain common friends, and afterward joined to me intimately in close companionship. He does everything attentively as regards my honour, anxiously as regards my health, cunningly as regards his love; for indeed he seemed to himself to have found a most suitable husband for his mother, to whom he might, with safe warrant, entrust the whole fortune of the house. And at first, indeed, sounding my will with covert words, since he saw me eager for the road and turned away from the matter of a wife, he begs me to stay at least a little while: that he wished to set out with me; that another winter must be waited out, on account of the heat and the wild beasts of the Syrtes, since my illness had robbed me of this one. He even wins from my Appii, by many entreaties, that I should be moved to his house, to his mother's; that the lodging would be healthier for me; and besides, that I should enjoy more freely from it the prospect of the sea, which is most pleasing to me.

All these things, striving with eager zeal, he carries; he commends to me his mother and his brother, this boy here. I help them not a little in our common studies; the familiarity grows greatly. Meanwhile I recover; at the request of friends I discourse somewhat in public; all who were present, filling the basilica, which was the place of the lecture, with a vast throng, among very many other most fitting things, cried out to me with one remarkable voice, begging that I should remain, that I should become a citizen of Oea. Presently, when the audience was dismissed, Pontianus, taking that for his starting-point, set upon me, interprets the consent of the public voice as a divine omen, and discloses that it is his plan, if I do not refuse, to join his mother — at whom very many gape — to me in marriage (since to me alone, he says, he trusts and entrusts everything); that, if I would not take up that burden — since it was no lovely young ward, but the mother of children, of middling looks, that was being offered me — if, weighing these things, I were keeping myself for another match for the sake of beauty and riches, I should be acting neither as a friend nor as a philosopher. It would be too long a speech, if I wished to recount what I answered to the contrary, how long and how often we bandied words between us, with how many and what kind of entreaties he set upon me, and did not let go before he at length prevailed — not but that I had already, by a whole year's constant intercourse, well observed Pudentilla and explored the endowments of her virtues, but inasmuch as, being desirous of travel, I had for a while refused the impediment of marriage. Soon, however, I wished for such a woman no less eagerly than if I had sought her of my own accord. Pontianus had also persuaded his mother to prefer me to all others, and was eager to accomplish this as soon as possible, with incredible zeal. Hardly could we win from him so much delay as this — that first he himself should take a wife, and his brother should take up the use of the manly toga; and then at length that we should be joined.

Would, by Hercules, that I could pass over what must next be said without the greatest loss to my case, lest I should seem now to be reproaching with fickleness Pontianus, whose error, when he deprecated it, I freely forgave. For I confess what has been thrown in my teeth: that, after he had taken a wife, he fell away from the faith of our compact, and, his mind suddenly changed, went about to hinder, with equal obstinacy, the very thing he had before hastened with excessive zeal — in short, that, to keep our marriage from coming together, he was ready to suffer anything, to do anything; although all that so foul a change of mind, and the quarrel undertaken against his mother, is not to be charged to his own fault, but to his father-in-law, that Herennius Rufinus yonder, who has left no single man on earth more worthless than himself, or more wicked, or more befouled. In few words, as moderately as I can, I will of necessity describe the man, lest, if I keep wholly silent about him, he should have lost his labour, who stirred up this business against me with his utmost might. For this is the instigator of this little boy, this the author of the accusation, this the hirer of advocates, this the buyer of witnesses, this the little furnace of the whole slander, this the firebrand and the lash of this Aemilianus; and he boasts of it, most intemperately, before everyone, that by his contrivance I have been arraigned as a defendant. And indeed he has, in these things, something to applaud himself for. For he is the cheat of all lawsuits, the deviser of all forgeries, the architect of all pretences, the seed-bed of all evils; and likewise the very den, the haunt, the brothel of lusts and gluttonies; from his earliest years openly notorious for all manner of disgrace; once, in his boyhood, before he was disfigured by that baldness, complaisant in every unspeakable thing to those who unmanned him; soon, in his youth, in dancing pantomimes, plainly boneless and nerveless, but, as I hear, with an untaught and clumsy effeminacy; for it is denied that he had anything of the actor about him except indecency.

Even at this age which he is now of — may the gods destroy him! much courtesy must be premised to your ears — his whole house is a pander's house, his whole household defiled: himself a thing of shame, his wife a she-wolf, his sons like them. Day and night, downright, his door is battered by the kicks of the youth in their sport, his windows are loud with serenades, his dining-room is in an uproar with revellers, his bedchamber lies open to adulterers; for no one has any fear of entering, except the man who has brought no price to the husband. Thus the dishonour of his own bed is his revenue. Once he made his money by his own body, now by his wife's, in the common market; with the man himself — and I do not lie — with the man himself, I say, very many strike their bargains for nights with his wife. Now there is that well-known collusion between husband and wife: those who have brought a generous fee to the woman, no one watches them, they depart at their own discretion; those who have come emptier, at a signal given are caught, as if for adulterers, and, as though they had come to learn a lesson, do not depart before they have written something. For what is a wretched man to do, fallen from a rather ample fortune, which yet he had unexpectedly come by through his father's fraud? His father, sunk in debt to very many creditors, preferred money to honour; for when he was dunned on every side with the account-books, and held, as if a madman, by all he met, "Peace!" said he, declares he cannot pay, throws away his golden rings and all the insignia of his rank, makes a composition with his creditors. Yet most of his estate he transfers, by a most cunning fraud, into his wife's name: himself needy, naked, and safe through his own ignominy, he left to this Rufinus — I do not lie — three hundred thousand sesterces to devour; for so much came to him, free and clear, out of his mother's goods, besides what his wife sought for him by her daily dowries. All which, however, in a few years, this glutton so diligently buried in his belly and squandered in revellings of every kind, that you would think he was afraid lest it be said he had anything left from his father's fraud; this just man, and of strict morals, took pains that what had been ill got should ill perish, and nothing was left him of his rather ample fortune except a wretched ambition and a bottomless gullet.

As for his wife, now nearly an old woman and worn out, she refuses to feed the whole house any longer by her shame; but his daughter, carried round in vain among the richer young men at her mother's invitation, and even handed over to certain suitors for trial, had perhaps, unless she had chanced upon the easy good nature of Pontianus, still been sitting at home a widow before she was a wife. Pontianus gave her — much against our dissuasion — the false and imaginary title of marriage, not unaware that a little before, when he was about to take her, she had been abandoned, after he had had his fill, by a certain most honourable young man, to whom she had previously been betrothed. So she came to him, the new bride, secure and undaunted, her modesty stripped off, her bloom faded, her bridal veil outworn — a virgin again after a recent divorce, bringing the name of a maiden rather than her intactness. She was carried in a litter of eight bearers; you certainly saw, you who were present, how shameless a scanner of the young men she was, how immoderate a displayer of herself. Who did not recognize the mother's training, when he saw in the girl her painted mouth, her rouged cheeks, her enticing eyes? Her whole dowry had been borrowed from a creditor, to the last farthing, the day before, and indeed a larger one than that exhausted house, full of children, could afford.

But this fellow, moderate as he is in substance, immoderate in hope, with avarice and want equally his portion, had already devoured, in empty anticipation, the whole four million of Pudentilla, and thinking that I must therefore be got out of the way, that he might the more easily circumvent the easy good nature of Pontianus and the loneliness of Pudentilla, begins to upbraid his son-in-law for having betrothed his mother to me; he advises him to draw back his foot, as soon as he can, from so great a peril, while it is permitted; to hold his mother's property himself rather than knowingly transmit it to a stranger; and, if he will not do so, the old hand throws a scruple into the love-sick youth, threatens that he will take his daughter away. What more? The simple young man, moreover bridled by the allurements of his new bride, he turns aside from the road at his own pleasure. He goes to his mother, the carrier of Rufinus's words; but, her gravity having been tried in vain, himself rebuked into the bargain for fickleness and inconstancy, he carries back to his father-in-law no soft answer: that to his mother, immovable apart from her most placid disposition, anger too had been added by his expostulation — no slight reinforcement of her steadfastness; that she had answered, in short, that it was not hidden from her that she was being remonstrated with at Rufinus's instigation; and that for that very reason she ought all the more to provide herself with a husband's aid against his desperate avarice.

On hearing this, that pimp of his own wife was so exasperated, swelled up with such anger, blazed with such frenzy, that against a most holy and most modest woman, in the presence of her own son, he spoke things worthy of his bedchamber, cried out that she was a wanton, that I was a magician and a poisoner, in the hearing of many (whom, if you will, I shall name): that he would bring death upon me with his own hand. Hardly, by Hercules, can I govern my anger; a huge indignation rises in my mind. You, you most effeminate of men, with your hand threaten death to any man? But with what hand, pray? That of Philomela, or Medea, or Clytemnestra? And yet, when you dance these — such is the softness of your soul, such your dread of steel — you dance them without a sword. But, not to digress too far from my order: Pudentilla, after she sees that her son, against expectation, has been perverted to the opposite of her own resolve, set out for the country and wrote to him, by way of rebuke, that most notorious letter, in which, as those men kept saying, she confessed that she had been led into love and madness by my magic; which letter, however, in the presence of Pontianus's clerk and with Aemilianus writing on the other side, we copied out, under attestation, the day before yesterday, by your command, Maximus; and in it everything is found, contrary to the proclamation of those men, in my favour.

And yet, even if she had called me a magician more roundly, she might be thought to have wished, by way of excuse to her son, rather to allege my compulsion than her own will. Or was Phaedra alone in inventing a false letter about love, and is not this an art familiar to all women — that, when they have begun to want anything of the kind, they prefer to seem compelled? But even if she really thought so in her heart, that I was a magician, am I therefore to be held a magician, because Pudentilla wrote this? You, with so many arguments, so many witnesses, with so long a speech, do not prove me a magician: would she prove it with a single word? And how much more weight, pray, is to be given to what is sworn to in a court than to what is written in a letter? Why do you not convict me by my own deeds, rather than by another's words? Otherwise, by the same road, many men will be arraigned for any crime you please, if whatever a man has written in his letter, out of love or hatred for someone, is to hold good. "Pudentilla wrote that you were a magician: therefore you are a magician." What if she had written that I was a consul: should I be a consul? What, if a painter, if a physician, what, finally, if innocent? Would you think me any of these, for the reason that she had said it? Nothing of the kind, of course. And yet it is most unjust to put faith, in the worse case, in one to whom you would not put it in the better — that her letter has power to ruin, but no power to save. "But," he says, "she was out of her mind, she loved you to distraction." I grant it for the moment. Are all those who are loved, then, magicians, if perchance the one who loves writes this? I believe rather, now, that Pudentilla at that time did not love me, since she wrote abroad what was plainly going to harm me.

Finally, which do you wish — that she was sane, or insane, when she wrote? You will say sane? Then she had suffered nothing from magic arts. You will answer insane? Then she did not know what she wrote, and therefore no faith is to be put in her; nay rather, if she had been insane, she would not have known that she was insane. For just as he acts absurdly who says that he is silent — since by saying so in that very place he does not keep silent, and by the very profession weakens what he professes — so this is even more self-contradictory: "I am insane," which is not true unless he says it knowingly; but he is sane who knows what insanity is, since insanity cannot know itself, any more than blindness can see itself. Therefore Pudentilla was of sound mind, if she did not think herself of sound mind. I could, if I wished, say more, but I let logic go. I will read the letter itself, which cries out something far different, and which seems, as it were, deliberately prepared and fitted for this trial. Take it, you, and read, until I interrupt. — Hold back a little while what follows; for we have come to a turning-point of the matter. For so far, Maximus, as far as I at least have observed, nowhere has the woman named magic, but she has gone over the same order which I went over a little before: of her long widowhood, of the remedy for her health, of her wish to marry, of my praises, which she had learned from Pontianus, of his own urging that she should marry me above all.

Thus far it has been read. There remains that part of the letter which, written likewise in my favour, turns its horns against my very self; which, sent with diligence to drive the charge of magic from me, by a memorable encomium of Rufinus has changed sides, and of its own accord sought to fix upon me the contrary opinion of certain people of Oea, as of a magician. Many things, Maximus, you have heard by report, more you have learned by reading, not a few you have ascertained by experience: but cunning so insidious, so compounded of marvellous villainy, you will deny that you ever came to know. What Palamedes, what Sisyphus, what Eurybates, finally, or Phrynondas could have devised the like? All those whom I have named, and any others besides who are memorable for guile, if they be set against this one piece of Rufinus's deceit, will plainly seem mere clowns and buffoons. O wonderful contrivance! O subtlety worthy of the prison and the rack! Who would believe it could be brought about that what had been a defence, the same — the same letters remaining — should be turned into an accusation? It is, by Hercules, incredible. But how this incredible thing was done, I will prove.

There was a mother's rebuke to her son, because he, taking it from Rufinus's opinion, now kept calling a magician me, such a man as she had proclaimed me to him. The very words ran in this manner: "Apuleius is a magician, and I have been bewitched by him and am in love. Come, then, to me, while I am still in my right mind." These very words, which I have inserted in Greek, Rufinus, alone excerpting them and sundered from their context, carried round as if it were the woman's confession, and, leading the weeping Pontianus through the forum, showed them to the crowd, offered the woman's very letter to be read just so far as I have said, and concealed the rest written above and below; he kept saying they were too shameful to be shown: it was enough that the woman's confession of magic should be known. What more? It seemed plausible to everyone; the very things that had been written to clear me roused against me a monstrous odium among the ignorant. This filthy fellow ranged through the middle of the forum, raving like a Bacchanal, again and again opening the letter and crying aloud: "Apuleius is a magician; she herself says what she feels and suffers; what more do you want?" There was no one to take my part and to answer thus: "Give us the whole letter, if you please; let me look at it all, let me read it through from beginning to end. There are many things which, brought forward alone, can seem liable to slander. Anyone's speech can be misrepresented, if those things which are linked to what went before are cheated of their beginning, if certain things are suppressed at pleasure out of the order of the writing, if things said for pretence are read with the delivery of one asserting rather than of one reproaching." These things, and the like of them, might then deservedly have been said; the very order of the letter shows it.

But you, Aemilianus, call to mind whether you copied out under attestation, along with me, these words too: "For, wishing to marry for the reasons I have stated, you yourself persuaded me to choose this man before all others, admiring the man and being eager to make him your own through me. But now, since malicious accusers are talking you over, suddenly Apuleius has become a magician, and I have been bewitched by him and am in love. Come, then, to me, while I am still in my right mind." I beseech you, Maximus: if letters, just as some are called vowels, had also a voice of their own; if words, as the poets say, flew abroad on wings — would not, the moment Rufinus in bad faith excerpted that letter, read a few words, knowingly kept silent about many and better ones, would not then the rest of the letters have cried out that they were being wickedly held back, would not the suppressed words have flown out of Rufinus's hands into the open, have filled the whole forum with their tumult: that they too had been sent by Pudentilla, that they too had been charged with things to say; that to a wicked and impious man, trying to commit a forgery through another's letter, they would not give ear, but would rather be heard themselves; that Apuleius had not been accused of magic by Pudentilla, but acquitted, with Rufinus for accuser? All which, even if they were not said then, yet now, when they are of more profit, appear clearer than the light. Your arts lie open, Rufinus, your frauds gape wide, the lie is uncovered: the truth, once perverted, now bears itself forth, and slander plunges, as into a deep pit.

You appealed to the letters of Pudentilla: by the letters I win; and if you wish to hear also their very last clause, I will not grudge it. Say, you, with what words the woman finished her letter — the bewitched, the senseless, the mad, the love-sick woman: "I am neither bewitched nor in love. I am escaping my destiny." Do you want still more? Pudentilla cries out against you, and vindicates her own sanity from your slanders by a kind of public proclamation; and the reason, or the necessity, of her marrying she ascribes to fate, from which magic is far removed, or rather wholly abolished. For what force is left to enchantments and poisons, if fate, like a most violent torrent, can neither be held back nor driven on? Therefore, by this sentence of hers, Pudentilla has denied not only that I am a magician, but that magic exists at all. It is well that Pontianus, after his custom, preserved his mother's letters whole; it is well that the haste of the trial forestalled you, lest you should make any change in these letters at your leisure. This, Maximus, is the benefit of you and of your foresight, that, having from the beginning understood the slanders, lest they should be strengthened by time, you precipitated them, and, granting no delay, hamstrung them. Suppose now that a mother had confessed to her son, in a secret letter, something about love, as is wont. Was it right, Rufinus — I do not say pious, but even merely humane — to publish those letters, and to publish them above all by the proclamation of her son? But am I not foolish, who demand that you preserve another's modesty, you who have lost your own?

But why do I complain of things past, when present things are no less bitter? To this point has that wretched boy been perverted by you, that he reads out his mother's letters, which he thinks amatory, before a proconsular tribunal, in the presence of that most holy man Claudius Maximus; that before these statues of the emperor Pius a son reproaches his mother with shameful debaucheries and throws her loves in her teeth. Who is so mild that he would not grow hot with anger? Do you, you basest of men, search out your parent's heart in such matters, watch her eyes, count her sighs, explore her affections, intercept her letters, convict her of love? Do you inquire what she does in her bedchamber, that your mother may be reckoned — I do not say a wanton, but not even a woman at all? Do you think of nothing in her but the single reverence due to a parent? O unhappy your womb, Pudentilla! O barrenness better than children! O ill-fated ten months! O thankless fourteen years of widowhood! The viper, as I hear, gnawing through its mother's womb, creeps forth into the light, and so is born by parricide: but to you, while you live and look on, harsher bites are offered by a son now grown up. Your silence is torn, your modesty is plucked, your breast is pierced, your inmost vitals are dragged forth. Are these the thanks, good son, that you repay your mother — for the life she gave, for the inheritance she acquired, for the long fourteen years of nurture? In these disciplines did your uncle school you, that, if you should learn for certain your sons would be like you, you would not dare to take a wife? There is a verse of the poet, not unknown: "I hate little boys of precocious wisdom." But a boy precocious in malice, who would not turn from and hate, when he sees, like a monster, one robust in crime before he is robust in years, harmful before he is powerful, with green boyhood, with hoary malice? Or rather, all the more noxious is this, that he is pernicious with impunity, and, not yet ripe for punishment, is already ripe for injury — injury, do I say? nay rather, for a crime against a parent, unspeakable, monstrous, intolerable.

The Athenians, indeed, for the common right of humanity, out of the captured letters of Philip of Macedon, their enemy, when each was being read in public, forbade one letter to be read out, which had been written to his wife Olympias; they spared the enemy rather than divulge a husband's secret, judging that the common law of right ought to be preferred to their own vengeance. Such were enemies toward an enemy: what kind of son are you toward a mother! You see how close are the things I compare. Yet you, a son, read your mother's letters, written about love, as you say, in this assembly — in which, if you were bidden to read some too-wanton poet, you would assuredly not dare; some shame, at least, would hold you back. Nay, you would never have touched your mother's letters, if you had touched any other letters at all. But how you dared to give to be read your own letter — which, written too irreverently, too insultingly and foully about your mother, while you were still being nursed in her bosom, you had sent secretly to Pontianus, no doubt that you might not have sinned only once, and that your good deed might be taken in by his gaze! Wretch, you do not understand that your uncle suffered this to be done in order to clear himself before men, if from your letter it should be known that you, even before you came over to him, even while you were fawning on your mother, were nevertheless already a sly fox and an impious one.

For the rest, I cannot bring myself to think Aemilianus so foolish as to suppose that the letters of a boy, and of one who is at the same time my accuser, will do me any harm.
