There was also that fabricated letter, neither written in my hand nor plausibly forged, by which they wished it to seem that the woman had been solicited by me with blandishments. Why should I use blandishments, if I trusted in magic? And by what way did the letter come to them — a letter sent, of course, to Pudentilla through some trusty person, as is wont to be done with care in such a matter? Why, besides, should I write in such faulty words, in so barbarous a style — I, whom those same men say is by no means unskilled in the Greek tongue? Why, again, should I court her with blandishments so absurd and so tavern-like — I, whom those same men say sport wittily enough in amatory verses? It is so, assuredly; it is plain to anyone: this man, who could not read Pudentilla's somewhat-too-Greek letter, read this one the more easily as his own, and commended it the more aptly. But I shall have said enough about the letters, if I add this one thing: that Pudentilla, who had written, by way of dissimulation and ridicule, "Come, then, while I am still in my right mind," after this letter summoned her sons and her daughter-in-law to her, and lived with them for about these two months. Let this pious son say what, in that time, he saw his mother do or say amiss through insanity; let him deny that she subscribed most shrewdly the accounts of the bailiffs and shepherds and grooms; let him deny that his brother Pontianus was gravely warned by her to beware of the snares of Rufinus; let him deny that he was truly rebuked because he had carried about the letter she had sent him among the crowd, and yet had not read it in good faith; let him deny that, after these things which I have mentioned, his mother married me at a country house, at a place agreed upon long before. For it had so pleased us, that we should rather be joined at a suburban villa, lest the citizens should again flock together for the doles, since not long before Pudentilla had paid out fifty thousand sesterces of her own to the people, on the day that Pontianus took a wife and this little boy was wrapped in the toga; and besides, that we might dispense with the many banquets and vexations which new husbands have, after custom, to undergo.

There you have, Aemilianus, the whole reason why the marriage-contract between me and Pudentilla was sealed not in the town, but at a suburban villa: lest fifty thousand sesterces should have to be lavished again, and lest we should have to dine with you or at your house. Is the reason adequate? Yet I wonder that you so shrink from a country house, you who for the most part live in the country. The Julian law on the marriages of the orders nowhere forbids in this fashion: "Thou shalt not take a wife at a country house"; nay, if you would have the truth, a wife is taken with much better auspices for offspring at a country house than in the town, on fertile soil rather than in a barren place, on the turf of the field rather than on the flag-stones of the forum. A woman about to be a mother, let her marry in the very lap of the mother, in the standing corn, upon the fruitful clod, or let her lie a bride beneath the elm, in the very bosom of mother Earth, among the offshoots of the grasses and the layered shoots of the vines and the buds of the trees. There too that most celebrated verse in the comedies aptly fits: "for the ploughing of lawful children, for the sowing." To the ancestors of the Romans also — the Quintii and the Serrani and many others like them — not only wives, but even consulships and dictatorships were offered in the fields. I will check myself in a theme so prolix, lest I do you a favour, if I should praise the country house.

But as to the age of Pudentilla, about which after these things you lied confidently enough, so that you said that she had married even at sixty years of age — about that I will answer you in few words; for there is no need, in a matter so plain, to dispute at length. Her father, after the manner of others, registered her at her birth as a daughter born to him. His records are kept partly in the public record-office, partly at home, and they are now thrust before your face. Hand these tablets, you, to Aemilianus: let him look at the thread, let him recognize the seals that are stamped upon it, let him read the consuls, let him reckon up the years which he was assigning, as sixty, to the woman. Let him prove fifty-five: then he has lied by five years. That is too little; I will deal more liberally — for he himself has bestowed many years upon Pudentilla, so I will give him back ten in turn: Mezentius has wandered along with Ulysses. Let him show the woman to be at least fifty years old. What more? That I may deal with the false-claimant, I will make twice the double of a five-year span, and at one stroke take off twenty years. Bid the consuls be reckoned, Maximus: unless I am mistaken, you will find that Pudentilla's age is now running on not much beyond the fortieth year. O bold and excessive falsehood, O lie to be punished with twenty years of exile! You lie by half as much again, Aemilianus, you dare a falsehood of one and a half times the truth. If you had said thirty years for ten, you might have seemed to err by the gesture of computation, by laying on the fingers which you ought to have curled into a circle. But when forty — which is more easily signified than the rest by the palm held out — when you increase these forty by half, you cannot have erred by the gesture of the fingers, unless perhaps, supposing Pudentilla to be thirty, you have counted the two consuls of each year.

These things I let pass. I come now to the very root of the accusation, to the very motive of the sorcery. Let Aemilianus and Rufinus answer: for what gain — even if I were the greatest of magicians — should I have enticed Pudentilla to marriage by charms and poisons? And I know that very many defendants, arraigned for some crime, if any motives have been proved to exist, have nevertheless defended themselves abundantly by this one plea — that their life shrinks far from crimes of this kind, and that it ought not to tell against them that there seem to have been certain inducements to the misdeed; for not all things that could have been done are to be held as done, and the changing turns of circumstance fall out variously: that the sure index of every man is his own mind; that he who has always, with the same disposition, been disposed toward virtue or toward malice, gives a firm argument for receiving or rejecting a charge. These things, although I could deservedly say them, yet I forgive you, and I do not think it enough for myself if I have abundantly cleared myself of all you have alleged, unless I have nowhere allowed even the slightest suspicion of magic to stand. Reckon with yourselves with what confidence in my innocence, and with what contempt of you, I act: if one motive, even the least, shall be found, why I should have sought the marriage of Pudentilla for some advantage of my own; if you prove any gain, however modest, then let me be that Carmendas, or Damigeron, or Moses, or Iannes, or Apollobex, or Dardanus himself, or whoever else after Zoroaster and Hostanes has been famous among the magicians.

See, I pray you, Maximus, what an uproar they have raised, because I have run over by name a few of the magicians. What am I to do with men so rude, so barbarous? Shall I teach them again that I have read these names, and many more besides, in the public libraries, among the most renowned writers? Or shall I argue that it is one thing to be acquainted with names, another to share in the art itself; and that the apparatus of learning and the memory of erudition ought not to be held a confession of crime? Or, what is far better, relying on your learning, Claudius Maximus, and on your perfect erudition, shall I scorn to answer the foolish and the unpolished on these points? Yes, I will do this rather: what they may think, I will count of no value; the thing I set out to do, I will go on to argue: that I had no motive for enticing Pudentilla to marriage by poisons. The woman's looks and age they themselves, of their own accord, disparaged, and laid it to my fault that, out of avarice, I had coveted such a wife, and indeed at our first meeting had seized a great and rich dowry. As to these things, Maximus, it is not my design to weary you with a long speech; no words are needed, since the very tablets speak far more eloquently, in which you find everything done at present and provided for the future, contrary to what those men, out of their rapacity, conjectured of me too: first of all, a modest dowry from a most wealthy woman, and that not given, but only entrusted on credit; and besides these things, that the union was made on this condition — that, if she should depart this life with no children begotten by me, the whole dowry should remain with her sons Pontianus and Pudens; but if she should die leaving one son or daughter surviving, then half the dowry should fall to the later child, the remainder to the elder ones.

These things, as I say, I will prove by the tablets themselves. Perhaps not even thus will Aemilianus believe that only three hundred thousand sesterces were set down, and the recovery of them given by compact to Pudentilla's sons. Take, if you please, these tablets with your own hands, give them to your instigator Rufinus: let him read, let him be ashamed of his swollen spirit and his ostentatious beggary; since he himself, needy and naked, dowered his daughter with four hundred thousand sesterces borrowed from a creditor, while Pudentilla, a wealthy woman, was content with a dowry of three hundred thousand, and has a husband who, scorning many and often vast dowries that were offered, was content with the empty name of so small a dowry, and reckons nothing but his wife, who puts all his furniture and all his riches in the concord of marriage and in mutual love. And yet who of all men, even slightly skilled in affairs, would dare to find fault if a widow, of middling looks but not of middling age, wishing to marry, had enticed by a long dowry and an easy condition a young man not to be regretted in body or mind or fortune? A beautiful maiden, even if she be downright poor, is yet abundantly dowered; for she brings to her husband a fresh disposition of soul, the grace of beauty, the first beginnings of bloom. The very recommendation of virginity is rightly and deservedly most acceptable to all husbands; for whatever else you have received as dowry, you can, when you please — so as not to be bound by the benefit — give back, just as you received it: repay the money, restore the slaves, move out of the house, withdraw from the estates: only virginity, once received, cannot be returned; it alone remains with the husband of the dowry-goods. But a widow, such as she came to the marriage, such she departs at the divorce; she brings nothing irrecoverable, but comes already deflowered by another, by no means apt to learn what you wish, no less suspicious of her new home than she is herself already to be suspected on account of that one divorce — whether she lost her husband by death, and so is a woman of ill omen and of unlucky marriage, by no means to be desired, or has parted by repudiation, a woman having either fault, who either was so intolerable as to be repudiated, or so insolent as to repudiate. For these and other reasons widows entice their suitors with an augmented dowry. Which Pudentilla too would have done in the case of another husband, had she not found a philosopher who scorned the dowry.

Come now: if I had coveted the woman for avarice's sake, what would have been more useful to me, for the possession of her house, than to sow discord between mother and sons, to alienate from her heart the affection of her children, that I might the more freely and closely possess the desolate woman alone? Was this the act of a robber — which you feign me to be? No, I was rather the author, the reconciler, the fosterer of quiet and concord and devotion; and not only did I sow no new hatreds, but I rooted out the old ones to their foundation. I urged my wife — whose whole resources, as those men say, I had already swallowed up — I urged her, I say, and at last persuaded her, that, when her sons demanded back their own money, of which I spoke above, she should restore that money without delay, in estates valued cheaply, and at whatever price they themselves wished; and besides, that out of her own estate she should give them the most fruitful fields and a great house richly furnished and a great quantity of wheat and barley and wine and oil and the other fruits, and slaves too, not fewer than four hundred, and cattle, neither few nor of mean value — that she might both make them secure as to that portion which she had assigned, and entice them, by hope, to the rest of the inheritance. These things, then, I wrung from an unwilling Pudentilla — for she will suffer me to tell it as the matter was — I extorted them from her, unwilling and angry, by mighty entreaties; I reconciled the mother to her sons, and enriched my stepsons, by this first benefit of a stepfather, with a great sum of money.

This was known to the whole city. All cursed Rufinus and extolled me with praises. Pontianus had come to us, before she completed that donation, together with that unlike brother of his, and, falling at our feet, had begged pardon and forgetfulness of all that was past, weeping and kissing our hands and saying that he repented of having listened to Rufinus and the like. He begs afterward, as a suppliant, that I would clear him also to Lollianus Avitus, a most distinguished man, to whom not long before he had been commended by me on the first trial of his oratory; for he had learned that, a few days before, I had written to him a full account of everything as it had happened. This too he obtains from me. And so, having received the letter, he sets out for Carthage, where Lollianus Avitus, his consulship now nearly run out, was awaiting you, Maximus. He, having read my letter, with his eminent humanity, congratulated Pontianus on having so quickly corrected his error, and wrote back to me by him a letter — good gods, with what learning, with what grace, with what charm and at the same time pleasantness of words, downright as a good man skilled in speaking. I know, Maximus, that you will gladly hear his letter; and indeed, if I read it aloud, I will pronounce it with my own voice. Hand over, you, the letters of Avitus, that what have always been an ornament to me may now be also a safeguard. But you may let the water-clock run on; for the letters of that excellent man I long to read over and over, three and four times, at whatever cost of time.

I am not unaware that, after these letters of Avitus, I ought to have brought my speech to a close. For what more wealthy eulogist, what more holy witness of my life, what more eloquent advocate, finally, could I produce? Many eloquent men of the Roman name I have diligently come to know in my life, but I have admired none equally. There is no one today, so far as my opinion goes, of any reputation or hope in eloquence, who would not far rather be Avitus, if, with envy set aside, he were willing to compare himself with him; for all the virtues of speaking, well-nigh opposite to each other, meet together in that man. Whatever speech Avitus has built, it will be so perfectly finished on every side that in it neither would Cato miss weight, nor Laelius smoothness, nor Gracchus impetuosity, nor Caesar fire, nor Hortensius arrangement, nor Calvus shrewdness, nor Sallust thrift, nor Cicero richness: in short — not to go through them all — if you hear Avitus, you would wish nothing added, nothing taken away, nor yet anything changed. I see, Maximus, how kindly you listen to what you recognize in your friend Avitus. Your courtesy invited me to say even these few things of him. But I will not so far indulge your good will as to allow myself, now almost wearied in a cause inclining downright toward its end, to begin only now upon his outstanding virtues; rather I will keep them for unspent strength and a free hour.

For now, much against my will, my speech must roll back from the commemoration of so great a man to those plagues. Do you dare, then, Aemilianus, to compare yourself with Avitus? Will you assail with the charge of magic and sorcery the man whom he calls a good man, the disposition of whose mind he praises so fully in his letter? Or ought you to grieve more that I invaded the house of Pudentilla and plundered her goods than Pontianus would have grieved — Pontianus, who, for the quarrels that arose between us over a few days, at your instigation, of course, made me satisfaction even in my absence before Avitus, who gave me thanks before so great a man? Suppose that I had read the proceedings before Avitus, not his own letter. What could you, or anyone, accuse in that business? Pontianus himself credited to my gift what he had received as a donation from his mother; Pontianus rejoiced with his inmost affections that I had fallen to him as a stepfather. Would that he had returned safe from Carthage! Or, since it had been so decreed for him by fate, would that you, Rufinus, had not hindered his last disposition. What thanks he would have given me, either to my face or at least in his will! Yet the letters which he sent ahead to me from Carthage, or even already on his way, from the road — while still in health, and already sick — full of honour, full of love, allow, I pray you, Maximus, to be read a little while, that his brother, my accuser, may know how, in everything inferior, he runs the course of his life beside his brother, a man of excellent memory.

Have you heard the titles which your brother Pontianus bestowed on me — calling me his parent, his lord, his master, both often at other times and especially at the very last period of his life, after . . . ? Your matching letters too I would bring forth, if I thought even a little delay worth so much. Rather I would wish to bring forward that recent will of your brother, which, though unfinished, yet most dutifully and most honourably makes mention of me. But that will Rufinus suffered neither to be drawn up nor to be completed, out of shame at the lost inheritance, which, as the price of the few months in which he was Pontianus's father-in-law, he had reckoned at a great rate of nights. Besides, he had consulted I know not what Chaldaeans, at what gain he should bestow his daughter, who — as I hear (and would they had not answered it truly) — replied first, that her husband would die within a few months; for the rest, about the inheritance, as is wont, they made up to the wish of the consulter. But, as the gods willed, like a blind beast he gaped in vain. For Pontianus, having found out the daughter of Rufinus to be of ill repute, not only did not leave her his heir, but did not even bestow on her an honourable legacy; indeed he ordered linens of about two hundred denarii to be assigned to her, by way of insult, that it might be understood that he had reckoned her in anger rather than passed her over in forgetfulness. He wrote as heirs, both in this will and in the former one which was read, his mother together with his brother; to whom, as you see, a boy still in years, Rufinus is applying that same machine of his daughter, and is thrusting some woman much older in years, the very lately wife of his brother, upon and beneath the wretched boy.

But he, captured and possessed by the blandishments of the harlot girl and the enticements of her pander of a father, the moment his brother gave up the ghost, left his mother and went over to his uncle, that the more easily, with us removed, the things begun might be accomplished; for Aemilianus favours Rufinus and desires the harvest. — Ha, you rightly remind me: the good uncle too tempers and fosters his own hope in this boy, knowing that of a child who dies intestate he will be the legal heir rather than the just one. I would not, by Hercules, that this had come from me; it was not part of my moderation to break openly the silent suspicions of all; you do wrong, who have prompted it. To be plain, indeed, if you would have the truth, many wonder, Aemilianus, at this so sudden affection of yours toward that boy, after his brother Pontianus is dead, when before you were so unknown to him that often you did not even recognize your brother's son by sight when you met him. But now you show yourself so indulgent to him, and so corrupt him with indulgence, you oppose him in nothing, that by these very things you give credit to the more suspicious. We received him unmanly: you have made him a man at once. While he was ruled by us, he went to his masters: from them he now flees in great flight into the cookshop, spurns serious friends, and, with the basest young men, among harlots and wine-cups, a boy of this age plies his banqueting. He himself is the ruler of your house, himself the master of the household, himself the master of the feast; at the gladiatorial school too a frequent visitor, he is taught the names of the gladiators and their fights and wounds — by the trainer himself, indeed, quite as becomes an honourable boy. He never speaks except Punic, and what he still keeps of Greek from his mother; for to speak Latin he neither will nor can. You heard, Maximus, a little while ago — O abomination! — my stepson, the brother of Pontianus, that eloquent young man, scarcely stammering out single syllables, when you asked him whether their mother had given them what I said had been given through my exertions.

I call you, then, to witness, Claudius Maximus, and you who sit in council, and you too who stand with me at the tribunal, that these losses and disgraces of his character are to be charged to this uncle here and to that candidate of a father-in-law; and that henceforth I shall count it well that such a stepson has shaken the yoke of my care from his neck, and that I shall not hereafter make supplication to his mother on his behalf. For — what I had very nearly forgotten — very lately, when Pudentilla, after the death of her son Pontianus, was making her will in ill health, I strove long against her, that she should not disinherit this boy on account of so many notable insults, so many injuries; that she should cancel a most grievous clause already, by Hercules, wholly written out, I begged with earnest entreaties; finally, that, if I should not prevail, I would part from her, I threatened: that she would grant me this favour, overcome a bad son by a benefit, free me from all envy. Nor did I desist before she did so. I am sorry that I have removed this scruple from Aemilianus, that I have disclosed to him a thing so unexpected. Behold, I pray you, Maximus, how, on hearing this, he was suddenly struck dumb, how he cast his eyes to the ground; for he had thought far otherwise, and not without reason: he knew the woman to be infected with her son's insults and bound to me by my services. Of me too there was something for him to fear: anyone, even though he scorned the inheritance as much as I, would yet not have refused to be avenged on so undutiful a stepson. This anxiety especially goaded them to accuse me: they falsely conjectured, out of their own avarice, that the whole inheritance had been left to me. I free you, as to the past, from that fear. For neither the occasion of inheritance nor of revenge could move my mind from its place. I fought with an angry mother on behalf of a bad stepson, a stepfather, as a father for the best of sons against a stepmother; nor was it enough, unless I restrained my good wife's lavish liberality toward me, far beyond what was fair.

Hand over, you, the will now made by the mother against her unfriendly son, with me — whom these men call a robber — dictating each single word along with entreaties. Bid these tablets be broken open, Maximus: you will find the son the heir, but to me indeed I know not what slight thing left for honour's sake, lest, if anything in the way of mortality should befall him, I, the husband, should not have my name in my wife's tablets. Take that will of your mother — undutiful, indeed, this one truly; and why not? — in which she disinherited a most obedient husband, and wrote as heir a most hostile son; nay rather, not a son, but the hopes of Aemilianus and the marriage of Rufinus, but that drunken company, your parasites. Take it, I say, best of sons, and, laying aside your mother's amatory letters a little while, read the will rather: if she wrote anything as one insane, you will find it here, and indeed at the very beginning: "Let Sicinius Pudens, my son, be my heir." I confess, whoever reads this will think her insane. This your son, heir — who, at the very funeral of his brother, with a band of most abandoned young men called in, wished to shut you out of the house which you yourself had given; who took it grievously and bitterly that you had been left coheir to him by his brother; who at once deserted you, with your grief and mourning, and fled to Rufinus and Aemilianus from your bosom; who afterward spoke very many insults to your face and, with his uncle aiding, committed them; who bandied your name about before the tribunals; who tried to disgrace your modesty publicly by your own letters; who arraigned on a capital charge your husband, whom you had chosen, whom, as he himself objected, you loved to distraction? Open, I pray you, good boy, open the will: so you will more easily prove your mother's insanity. Why do you refuse, why do you decline, now that you have repelled your anxiety about your mother's inheritance? But I, these tablets,

Maximus, here on the very spot, before your feet, I throw down, and I call you to witness that henceforth I shall hold it of less concern what Pudentilla writes in her will. Let him himself now, as he pleases, entreat his mother for the rest: for me, he has left no room to plead further on his behalf. Let him himself now — being his own master, and a man who dictates most bitter letters to his mother — soften her anger; he who could plead a cause to the end will be able to plead a prayer to good effect. For me it is long since enough, if I have not only most fully dissolved the charges brought against me, but have even rooted up, to its foundation, the very root of this trial — that is, the envy of inheritance sought. This too, lest I pass over any of the whole, before I close, I will refute as falsely alleged. You said that I had bought, in my own name, a most beautiful estate with a great sum of the woman's money. I say it was a tiny little inheritance of sixty thousand sesterces; that, moreover, not I, but Pudentilla bought it in her own name; that Pudentilla's name is in the tablets; that the tax for that little field was paid in Pudentilla's name. The public quaestor is present, to whom it was paid, Corvinius Celer, a man of distinction; the woman's guardian and authorizer is here too, a man most grave and most holy, to be named by me with every honour, Cassius Longinus. Ask, Maximus, of what purchase he was the authorizer, at what trifling price the wealthy woman bought her little field. Is it as I said? Is my name written in anywhere in this purchase? Is the very price of the little inheritance a matter of envy? Was even this, at least, bestowed on me?

What else is there, Aemilianus, that I have not refuted with you for judge? What reward of my magic have you found? Why, then, should I bend Pudentilla's mind by poisons? That I might take what advantage from her? That she should name me a modest dowry rather than an ample one? O glorious charms! Or that she should bind back that dowry to her sons rather than leave it with me? What can be added to this magic? Or that, at my urging, she should give away most of her estate to her sons — she who, before me as husband, had bestowed nothing on them — and impart nothing whatever to me? O grievous sorcery — shall I call it? — or thankless benefit. Or that, in the will she was writing in anger against her son, she should leave as heir the son with whom she was offended, rather than me, to whom she was bound? This indeed I obtained with difficulty, by many enchantments. Suppose that you were pleading your cause not before Claudius Maximus, a man fair and tenacious of justice, but set up some other depraved and savage judge, a favourer of accusations, eager to condemn: give him something to go on, supply even the least plausible occasion of pronouncing in your favour; at least invent something, devise what you might answer to the man who asked you this. And since every attempt must be preceded by some motive, answer, you who say that Apuleius assailed Pudentilla's mind with magic enticements: what did he seek from her, why did he do it? Had he desired her beauty? You deny it. Had he at least coveted her riches? The dowry-tablets deny it, the donation-tablets deny it, the will-tablets deny it — in which it is shown that he not only did not greedily reach after, but even harshly repelled, the liberality of his own wife. What other motive is there, then? Why have you fallen dumb? Why are you silent? Where is that savage opening of your indictment, framed in the name of my stepson:

"This man, my lord Maximus, did I set about making a defendant before you?" Why, then, do you not add: a defendant who is a teacher, a defendant who is a stepfather, a defendant who is an intercessor? But what next? "Of very many sorceries, and of the most manifest." Give me one out of the many; give me a doubtful one, or at least an obscure one, out of the most manifest. For the rest, to these things which you have objected, count whether I do not answer in a couple of words each. You polish your teeth: pardon a man his cleanliness. You look into mirrors: a philosopher ought to. You make verses: it is allowed to be done. You investigate fishes: Aristotle teaches it. You consecrate wood: Plato counsels it. You take a wife: the laws command it. She is older in years than you: it commonly happens. You went after gain: take the dowry-deed, recall the donation, read the will. And if I have beaten back all these things to the full, if I have refuted all the slanders, if in all things — not only the charges, but even the insults — I keep myself far from blame; if the honour of philosophy, which is dearer to me than my own safety, I have nowhere diminished, but rather, on the contrary, have everywhere held it fast with full sail: if these things, as I say, are so, then I can with an untroubled mind reverence your good opinion rather than dread your power, since I judge it less grievous and less to be feared to be condemned by a proconsul than, if I were disapproved by so good and so faultless a man. I have spoken.
